item.title: What Your GPS Knows About Friendship
item.description:
Friends

What Your GPS Knows About Friendship

Compassion isn't silence about wrong turns; it's honest redirection without contempt.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • A GPS treats every mistake as a new starting point, not as evidence against the driver.
  • Judgment after a mistake produces shame—and shame makes people hide, not correct course.
  • People are more able to change when mistakes can be acknowledged without their worth being placed on trial.

I am, by any measure, an average and careful driver. I treat speed limits almost religiously; on highways I set the cruise control two or three miles below the limit and leave it there. And I rely entirely on my car's navigation.

Still, there are days when I lose myself in my thoughts and miss a turn. And every single time, the same thing happens: no sigh, no lecture, no disappointment. The screen pauses for a moment—recalculating—and then offers me the best possible route from exactly where I now am.

One day it occurred to me: Imagine if the navigation behaved the way many of us do when someone we love makes a mistake.

"Why did you miss that turn? I told you about it half a mile ago." "That's the third time this month." "Honestly, I don't know why I bother giving you directions at all." We would turn that device off within a week. Yet this is precisely the voice that many of us offer a friend, a partner, a child, a sibling—which is to say, the people whose journeys matter to us most—at the very moment they have lost their way.

What the Navigation Actually Does

Look closely at the machine's behavior, because it follows four quiet principles.

  • It accepts your current position as the new starting point. There is no litigation of the past, no inquiry into why you are where you are. You are here; that is the only fact it needs.
  • It never downgrades your destination. A missed turn does not cause it to conclude that you no longer deserve to arrive. The destination stands; only the route changes.
  • It advises from where you are, not from where you should have been. Its guidance is always about the next turn—the one still available to you.
  • And it offers unlimited recalculations. There is no strike count, no accumulating file of your errors, no moment when it declares you hopeless and goes silent.

Acceptance of the present, faith in the destination, guidance toward the next right step, and no ledger of past failures. Read that list again slowly, and you may notice you have just read a fairly good definition of compassion.

Why Judgment Fails Where Recalculation Works

This is more than a charming metaphor; it matches what psychology knows about how people actually change.

Carl Rogers argued that the essential soil of personal growth is unconditional positive regard: being accepted without conditions of worth, so that a person's energy can go toward changing rather than toward defending themselves (Rogers, 1957). The navigation grants exactly this. Your worth as a driver is never on the table; only your route is.

article continues after advertisement

Judgment can produce shame—and shame research helps explain why that may backfire. Shame condemns the self rather than the act and is associated with hiding, defensiveness, and avoidance—responses that interfere with acknowledgment and repair (Tangney et al., 2007). The friend who feels judged for missing a turn does not navigate better. They stop telling you where they are—which is the one piece of information any guidance depends on.

The same logic applies to the voice we use on ourselves. Self-compassion offers a similar inner posture: acknowledging failure without self-condemnation and returning attention to the next constructive step, rather than overidentifying with the mistake (Neff, 2003). "Recalculating" turns out to be a healthier inner monologue than "How could you be so stupid?"

Compassion Is Not Silence

One clarification matters. The navigation is not permissive. It does not pretend the wrong road is fine, and when I am genuinely headed the wrong way, it tells me plainly: Make a U-turn. Compassion, likewise, is not the absence of honesty. It is honesty stripped of contempt—truthful redirection that never turns a wrong turn into a wrong person: "I love you, and this path is hurting you," not "You are ruining your life."

That distinction is the whole art of being a real friend to someone who is lost: to say clearly, "This road doesn't lead where you want to go," while communicating just as clearly, "and your destination still stands, and I am still navigating with you."

One more honest difference between machines and people: Human friendship requires boundaries. A GPS cannot be harmed by the driver's choices; a friend can. Caring about someone's destination does not obligate us to accompany every route they choose—especially when their choices repeatedly harm themselves or others. Compassion can remain fully intact even when boundaries become necessary.

Recalculating

So perhaps this is the definition I have been circling: Compassion is the refusal to prosecute someone for being lost, combined with an honest effort to understand where they are and help them find the next constructive turn. A real friend is a human GPS: You are here. You still want to go there. Here is the next right turn. I am with you.

article continues after advertisement

The next time someone you love misses a turn—forgets, relapses, fails, chooses badly—notice the sentence forming in your mind. If it begins with "Why" or "Again," pause for the length of one breath. Then do what the machine on your dashboard has been modeling for you all along.

Recalculate.

item.title: When Caring for Mom or Dad Divides a Family
item.description:
Caregiving

When Caring for Mom or Dad Divides a Family

A new survey finds that the stress of caring for aging parents can break sibling bonds.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • One in five people report experiencing permanent sibling estrangement due to careing for an aging parent.
  • Nearly half of caregivers report that they resent a sibling because caregiving was not shared fairly.
  • Gender expectations can shape how families divide care; daughters are typically the hands-on caregiver.
  • A family text thread may be convenient for quick updates, but it can also intensify conflict.
Source: Yaroslav-shuraev/pexels

When a parent falls ill, siblings – some of whom may not have had much contact in recent years – are suddenly thrown together again and required to avoid falling into old family patterns, transcend their differences, and make critical decisions together to care for an aging mom or dad. A new study has found that this scenario places terrible pressure on the sibling relationship, often resulting in estrangement.

Caregiving often arrives at a life stage when adult children already are overwhelmed with raising their kids, trying to build or maintain their careers, paying mortgages, managing households, caring for spouses, or navigating their own health concerns. The result is a pressure cooker: Practical tasks pile up, emotions run high, and caregiving siblings measure each other’s contributions in time, money, attention, and sacrifice.

A new study (June 2026) commissioned by Bay Alarm Medical, a provider of medical alert systems and senior safety solutions, surveyed 1008 U.S. adults who share or once shared caregiving responsibility for a parent over 65. One of the most surprising findings is that 18 percent reported that they had lost a relationship with a sibling because of disagreements over caring for an aging parent.

“Family conflict is common,” says Ricardo Rodriguez of Fractl, a digital marketing agency. "However, the fact that almost one in five people experienced permanent estrangement from this situation is noteworthy.”

The survey also found that 28 percent of respondents were so frustrated that they were willing to cut off a sibling over disagreements about a parent’s care, medical appointments, safety, finances, housing, and daily support. Many factors play into these decisions, including a parent’s well-being, a family’s resources, and the emotional labor of watching someone age or decline.

Rodriguez says that the results of the survey show the high stakes of these decisions for siblings: “Seven in ten respondents (69 percent) reported having engaged in a fight with their siblings due to caregiving issues related to finances (36 percent) and unequal time spent on caregiving (26 percent).”

It’s Not Fair!

The study reveals that a perception of unfairness is often the catalyst for the conflicts. Nearly half of respondents (47 percent) said they feel resentment toward a sibling because caregiving is not shared equitably. Many families never discuss caregiving or create a thoughtful, carefully divided plan. Instead, caregiving often happens by default, based upon who lives closest, who has the more flexible job, or even who was the "favorite." Long-standing familiar sibling roles rooted in birth order, personality, and finances may emerge again, determining who steps forward and who steps back.

Gender expectations appear to shape how families divide care. The average caregiver says that one person shoulders 53 percent of the parent’s care responsibilities – making the appointments, driving to visits, coordinating medications, checking in daily, or managing emergencies — and typically, that person is a daughter. The survey found that 46 percent of respondents said a daughter carried the hands-on caregiving, nearly three times as many (17 percent) as those who said a son did. Meanwhile, less-involved siblings may feel criticized, excluded, or unaware of the amount of time and effort a sibling is devoting to caregiving.

It’s no surprise that this imbalance is fertile ground for animosity. “This disproportion,” Rodriguez says, “is likely one of the main reasons why almost half of the respondents are resentful.” Caregiving can turn small frustrations into larger conclusions about fairness, respect, and love. Some say the experience revealed a sibling's true character and their willingness to sacrifice for the family.

The Perilous Family Chat

Much of the communication and conflicts of caregiving occur in family chats. Half of respondents said that arguments happen in the family group chat. The number-one source of conflict, according to the survey, is money, followed by the imbalance of time and effort.

The family text thread is convenient for quick updates, but it can also intensify conflict as it's easy to misread tone and meaning. An exhausted sibling may fire off a hostile message about missed appointments or unpaid bills. Another may quickly respond defensively. Others may stay silent, which can be interpreted as indifference. Frustration can spread fast and, suddenly, the entire family is dragged into a disagreement before anyone has had time to cool down.

How to Reduce Conflict

Rodriguez says that the results of the research show that family trends are exacerbated by caregiving activities. Caregiving will always bring hard decisions, but siblings can reduce conflict by talking earlier, defining expectations clearly, and recognizing that care can take many forms. He offers these practical strategies to help families reduce conflict during the caregiving process:

  • Talk about roles ahead of time, and be open and honest about expectations.

  • Define roles clearly. Assigning specific duties (e.g., money management, driving, appointments, or everyday tasks) might help avoid confusion or misunderstandings.

  • Acknowledge what everyone is doing to minimize resentment. Each sibling may offer caregiving in different ways. For example, one may take care of everyday needs, another might be contributing financially, and yet another might schedule appointments.

  • Communicate directly. Given that many arguments occur in group messages, families may prefer to discuss difficult topics by phone or even face-to-face.

If caregiving or end-of-life disputes become too acrimonious, siblings can hire an “elder mediator.” This new field has emerged to respond to the needs of quarreling siblings, and these mediators help resolve issues such as caregiving, inheritance, living arrangements, and estate planning.

item.title: The Struggling Adult Child Wish Parents Feel Ashamed of
item.description:
Parenting

The Struggling Adult Child Wish Parents Feel Ashamed of

Why wanting your adult child to need you less can feel like a betrayal.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Parents' inner desire for relief is not betrayal. It is exhaustion.
  • Fixating on their child's label (e.g., "lazy" or "ADHD") may keep parents from exploring new ways to cope.
  • Moving from "I know why he's stuck" to curiosity ("What is he actually afraid of?") creates a sense of hope.

A mother I've been coaching said something to me last month that she'd clearly never said to anyone else. We were about 20 minutes into the session, talking through her 27-year-old son's third failed attempt at holding a job, when she stopped mid-sentence and said, "Honestly? I just wish I didn't have to think about him every day." Then she apologized for saying it.

I hear versions of this constantly from parents of struggling adult children. It's rarely the first thing they tell me—usually it comes out after they've already walked me through the diagnosis/condition/descriptive label they've settled on for their son or daughter. For example, he's got undiagnosed attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or he's depressed (again), he's just lazy, or she was always the difficult one (the parent who said this was grimacing). The label that seems to fit and explain everything, whether it came easily or has been elusive for a long time, is often the focus for frustrated parents of struggling adult children.

Parents Who Want Relief Feel Like They Are Abandoning Their Adult Children

Behind that label, many parents share with me the long list of setbacks and pain their adult children have experienced. Yet they seem to feel that their own wish for relief to make their lives as parents better is a taboo subject. It's as if the parents wanting to personally feel less pain and pressure is a betrayal to their adult child, especially if that adult child is blaming their parents for their own life's struggles.

I sought to address these feelings of enduring guilt and shame when I wrote my recent book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! I examined why wanting your adult child to need you less feels, to many parents, like a betrayal. And, repeatedly unhealthy levels of guilt (often activated by what adult children—who are in their own pain—say and do). But in my experience, it's the opposite. It's usually a sign that someone has been running on empty for a long time and hasn't had anywhere to put that down.

Shifting From the Need for Certainty to Curiosity Helps Many Parents

What I try to do in those sessions is to get parents to set the diagnosis, emotional limitations and struggles, blame-laden allegations against the parents, and that incessant, painful sense of guilt aside for a minute. Not forever, just long enough to ask a different question. Instead of "Why is he like this," try "What is he actually afraid of right now?" Instead of "She's taking advantage of me," try "What does she think happens if I stop?" That shift, from certainty to curiosity, is where I've seen the most movement happen, both in how parents feel and in what actually changes at home.

None of this means dropping boundaries or excusing harmful behavior. It means letting yourself want your own life back without treating that want as proof you're a bad parent. You can be exhausted and still show up. You can wish for quiet and still love your kid completely. Those two things were never actually in conflict—they just get talked about like they are.

article continues after advertisement

The Takeaway

If there's a wish like that sitting in you, the first move isn't fixing your adult child. It's about admitting to yourself first what you actually need. That's not selfish. In my experience, it's usually the thing that finally gets parents unstuck.

item.title: Surviving Moral Injury in Law Enforcement
item.description:
Moral Injury

Surviving Moral Injury in Law Enforcement

Why jumping right back into uniform might not be the best idea.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Moral injury (MI) occurs when committing or observing actions that go against one's moral principles.
  • Moral injury can prompt internalized feelings of anger, worthlessness, guilt, and shame.
  • Due to an overlap of MI and PTSD, social workers can use trauma-focused interventions to address MI.

Moral injury occurs when someone is exposed to actions or inaction that conflict with their moral beliefs. Ideally, recovery from moral injury on the job includes an ability to separate self-worth and occupation. Disentangling the person from the professional persona facilitates personal development and authenticity, as opposed to highlighting the identity that collapsed as a result of a professional mistake or mishap. Stepping out of the uniform after moral injury is often a relief for someone struggling after trauma, affording time for careful consideration of whether or when to step back in. Supportive friends, family, faith leaders, and colleagues can help someone struggling with moral injury by affirming authentic self-worth outside of the occupation that contributed to their emotional injury.

Source: BodyWorn by Utility / Pixabay

Experiencing and Recovering From Moral Injury

Some people do not “recover” from moral injury; they learn to live with it. There should be no burdensome pressure to overcome or overpower traumatic thoughts; getting through each day can be its own victory. And with respect to returning to the profession that caused the trauma, some people decide to jump right back into uniform, and others decide to hang it up and forge a new path. Either way, research reveals some helpful concepts to consider.

Kayla R. Hanley (2025) examined the co-occurrence of moral injury and PTSD in male police officers.[i] She begins by noting that a police officer who experiences a potentially morally injurious event (PMIE) is at risk for suffering moral injury (MI) if the officer does not have an opportunity to process the event with the help of a support system. She notes that MI involves a contrast between actions or inactions, and morality.

Exposure to Potentially Morally Injurious Events

Hanley defines MI for police officers as occurring when officers are “directly involved in or observe actions that go against their moral principles.” She notes MI is common yet under-researched as it occurs for police officers in urban areas, who witness or experience potentially morally injurious events (PMIE) at higher rates than persons not involved in law enforcement. MI can prompt internalized feelings of anger, worthlessness, guilt and shame, and feeling powerless. If unaddressed, MI can adversely impact officers through evolving into other mental health issues, such as increased rates of PTSD.

When left unaddressed, Hanley notes that someone can suffer from both MI and PTSD simultaneously. Although there is currently no evidence-based intervention for police officers who are experiencing MI, Hanley notes that because of the clinical overlap and frequent co-occurrence between MI and PTSD, social workers can use trauma-focused interventions to address MI.

Protective Factors and Peer Support

People suffering from adverse emotional symptoms can gain comfort from trusted family and friends, and professional help when appropriate. Hanley identifies factors that can protect officers from experiencing a PMIE (and possibly PTSD if the MI is left unaddressed) as including spiritual or religious connections, as well as self-forgiveness post PMIE, especially after an act of commission. She also notes that officers with strong social connections who discuss the PMIE with their support systems are less likely to develop MI. Together, these protective factors help to mitigate both MI and PTSD from developing in the first place.

Hanley concludes by observing the need for law enforcement agencies along with officers to normalize the experience of PMIEs on the job, while also supporting the officers who experience them, in order to reduce the impacts of MI.
